item.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

- Date:

- November 22, 2026

- Source:

- Estonian Research Council

- Summary:

- Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial âfingerprintsâ long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

- Share:

Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.

The gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the new findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.

To investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.

Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria

The findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.

These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.

"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as important as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," said Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.

This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone currently takes may overlook an important part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.

Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics

One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.

Researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.

The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.

This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.

Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped

To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.

By examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.

Although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.

Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought

The findings point to an important consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.

If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.

The results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.

"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data."

item.title: Earth just saw the most anomalously hot day ever on record
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Earth just saw the most anomalously hot day ever measured on the planet. According to preliminary data from the Europe-based Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), Friday, November 20, 2026 was 2.12 degrees Celsius higher than the preindustrial average—or the time before human's began heating up the Earth by burning fossil fuels.

The record stems from a combination of long-term, human-driven climate change and a blockbuster El Niño that is likely the strongest in the past 1,000 years. It come as international negotiations at the COP 31 climate summit fell apart, with no global agreement on how to rein in global warming.

On supporting science journalism

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

There are likely to be more days with an anomaly at or above 2 degrees C as this El Niño builds to its crescendo over roughly the next month. The next several months are also likely to be record hot. "I think we will likely see more days exceeding 2 degrees C over the next couple of months (possibly through March 2027)," says Zachary Labe, a scientist at Climate Central, a climate research nonprofit. "Though I still expect this to be more a rarity than the norm when comparing every day"

It's possible 2026 will be the hottest year on record, besting 2024, though it will be close and could end in a tie. Because it takes time for the heat released by El Niño in the Pacific to affect global temperatures, 2027 will likely see the biggest heat effect and will almost certainly become the hottest year on record. Both 2026 and 2027 will be more than 1.5 degrees C above preindustrial temperatures, a level so far only ever surpassed in 2024.

Under the landmark 2015 Paris climate agreement, which came out of the COP 21 meeting, countries agreed to limit warming to "well below" 2 degrees C above preindustrial and to try to keep it under 1.5 degrees C. But the United Nations (UN) recently announced that the world will blow past the 1.5 degrees C mark, with global temperatures expected to hit 1.8 degrees C above preindustrial.

Surpassing the 2 degrees C benchmark for a day—or even a year—doesn't mean the Paris agreement limit has been permanently breached, as that considers the average temperature over many years. By that measure, the world has warmed by nearly 1.4 degrees C above preindustrial, according to the UN.

The COP31 summit—to which the U.S. did not send an official delegation—ended without an agreement for a final deal. These documents nominally provide a blueprint for countries to follow in their efforts to lower greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the changing climate.

In a statement, outgoing Secretary General Antonio Guterres, who has been a vocal supporter of phasing out fossil fuels, noted his "profound frustration" at the summit's outcome. "Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly," Guterres said. "The world is now poised to exceed the globally-agreed limit of a 1.5 degree temperature rise. The window to keep that overshoot as short and shallow as possible is rapidly closing."

item.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimerâs risk, major review finds

- November 22, 2026

- Source:

- Curtin University

- Summary:

- People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimerâs disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimerâs each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently new cases occur.

Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

Unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi said.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes."

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

item.title: New Species of Flying Frog Discovered in Indonesia
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

New species can be discovered in all sorts of ways. In the case of Rhacophorus kurniatia, a type of Asian flying frog that’s only just been identified, it involved a trek deep into the Mekongga Mountains in Indonesia, to a secluded lake where thousands of frogs had congregated.

“We were moving up the mountain, and we came across this big pond covered in these green frogs,” Alan Hitch, one of the authors of a new study about Rhacophorus kurniatia, explained in a statement. “They were all over. You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that. This was something super special.”

They were quickly identified as being flying frogs, from the Rhacophorus genus. The large webbed feet, for gliding between trees, were the main giveaway. Further analysis revealed something not seen in other Rhacophorus species, though: The frogs deposit their eggs in gelatinous masses hanging above or near water, rather than in the typical foamy nests.

Distinctive, pointed snouts, as well as differences in the calls made by the frogs, confirmed that this was a species that hadn’t been observed and documented before.

“The team looked at hundreds and hundreds of specimens of frogs to describe the new species,” study author Andrew Engilis Jr. said in a statement. “Sometimes species can look the same, but their behavior is different and their genetics are different—these are called cryptic species. This frog is an example of that. It looks very similar to other Rhacophorus, but its genetics and behavior show that it’s very distinctive.”

The identification of R. kurniatia is the culmination of four years of work on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, which is close to Borneo. Expeditions carried out by the researchers led them from sea level to the highest mountain peaks—with the new flying frog species discovered some 6,100 feet above sea level.

And there’s a bittersweet reason for the naming: The flying frog’s scientific name was chosen as a mark of respect for renowned herpetologist Hellen Kurniati, who died in 2024. She was one of the leading researchers studying amphibians and reptiles in Indonesia. She also helped to discover the new species that now shares her name.

item.title: JWST finds a possible black hole that grew faster than its host galaxy in the early universe
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

November 22, 2026 report

JWST finds a possible black hole that grew faster than its host galaxy in the early universe

Shreejaya Karantha

Author

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

How the first massive black holes formed in the universe remains an open question in astronomy. Black holes weighing about a billion solar masses within the first billion years of the universe require extraordinary origin stories.

Now, a new multiwavelength study of a potential black hole may offer a clue. Combining spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) with Hubble imaging and archival data from the Very Large Telescope's MUSE instrument, astronomers identified this black hole in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy as seen about 12 billion years ago. This black hole appears to have a mass of about 3.3 million suns and sits in a galaxy containing roughly 145 million solar masses in stars. The discovery paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server, explains why this is unusual.

Overmassive black holes

Many recent studies have revealed early black holes that have a different relationship with their host galaxies, compared to what's seen in the nearby universe. Early black holes are too heavy compared to their host galaxies' stellar masses. This suggests the black holes in the early universe may grow quicker than the stars.

Researchers point out another factor that may affect the 'overmassive black holes' sample. Surveys can only detect black holes that are bright or fast-moving enough, so the samples have the heaviest ones for a given galaxy mass. Those giant black holes are only the tip of the iceberg. To really understand how black holes form and grow, astronomers need to look for the smaller, more typical ones too. But these are also hard to detect.

The signals from supernovae exploding into dense gas, shocks, and outflows can mimic faint black holes. In young, metal-poor galaxies, the spectral line ratios used to differentiate black hole-powered gas from star-powered gas may overlap, and extreme stars can mimic an active galactic nucleus (AGN), a galaxy powered by a massive black hole.

'Outpaced' growth

In the new study, Mirko Curti of the INAF—Astrophysics and Space Science Observatory of Bologna and colleagues used many lines of evidence rather than one to ask whether the object at the center of MARTA 3887 is an overmassive black hole.

Using the spectroscopic observations from JWST, they detected a wide hydrogen-alpha line, which revealed that the gas is moving at about 1,270 kilometers per second (790 miles per second). The signal appeared only in hydrogen, not in other kinds of lines such as those from oxygen that come from calmer gas. This pointed to a black hole rather than an ordinary outflow.

Next, they estimated the black hole's mass: roughly 3.3 million times the sun's mass. This mass estimate places it among the lower-mass black holes found by JWST. The galaxy, on the other hand, has about 145 million solar masses of stars, so the black hole is roughly 2.3% of the stellar mass.

Researchers note that this relation is "approximately 2 dex above the local relation," which means it is about 100 times higher than the relationship extrapolated from nearby galaxies. This suggests that "black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed stellar component," the team writes in the paper.

The galaxy itself is compact and clumpy and is low in heavy elements, about 10% of the sun's level, which is typical of a young galaxy. It is forming stars fast, roughly five to nine solar masses of new stars per year, mostly in a recent burst.

Growth tracking

The researchers then explored how the 'outpacing' could have happened. They built simple growth trackers assuming one black hole grows steadily from a seed, with no mergers, at a constant feeding rate. Each track was set to end at the measured mass at the time they observed the galaxy.

They found that if black hole growth began very early, when the universe was about 0.1 billion years old, the seeds with masses of 100, 10,000, and 100,000 suns would need to feed at about 34%, 19%, and 11% of the maximum rate. If growth began only with the recent star-formation burst, a 100-solar-mass seed would need to feed at about 570% of the maximum rate, which is extreme. This means a small black-hole seed that began its growth later would require strongly super-Eddington growth, while a more massive initial seed could grow more slowly.

The team is careful to note that this galaxy 'possibly' hosts a black hole. An interacting supernova or a compact and thick outflow could still mimic the signal, though these explanations are less likely. They cannot rule out these scenarios from data gathered during a single observation.

A possible 'leaker'

The galaxy may also be leaking ultraviolet light. Some of the high-energy ultraviolet photons from early galaxies had to escape into space to help clear the neutral hydrogen fog of the early universe during the cosmic reionization period. Several signs suggest MARTA 3887 has porous gas through which such light could escape. About 44% of the Lyman-alpha light produced by the galaxy escapes, which is a high fraction. Because they cannot yet measure the escape fraction of the ultraviolet photons, the team calls MARTA 3887 an indirect "leaker candidate."

Overall, this black hole candidate extends the individually detected population of actively feeding black holes into the faint, metal-poor, low-mass host regime, and suggests that its growth may have outpaced the buildup of its stars.

item.title: Silver briefly forms a rare crystal structure seen in radioactive polonium
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

Silver briefly forms a rare crystal structure seen in radioactive polonium

How atoms are arranged in a material shapes many of its properties. The same carbon atoms, for example, can form diamond and graphite depending on how they are arranged, giving rise to materials with vastly different chemical and physical properties. Now, researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a new crystal structure of silver with unusually high chemical reactivity. The findings, published in Nano Letters, could open new avenues for exploring materials with desirable properties.

Silver normally forms a repeating cube-shaped structure, with atoms located at each of the cube's eight corners and at the center of each face. This arrangement is known as a face-centered cubic crystal structure and is common among metals, including aluminum, copper and gold. In the new study, researchers observed that under certain conditions, silver atoms can adopt a simple cubic structure, in which the atoms occupy only the eight corners of a cube that repeats in three dimensions.

Simple cubic structures are exceptionally rare among elements. One other example is the radioactive element polonium.

In this study, researchers used an electron beam to trigger the decomposition of silver iodide, observing the newly formed silver atoms arrange themselves into a previously unreported simple cubic structure.

At the nanoscale, where materials measure just a few billionths of a meter, structures that are unstable in larger materials can sometimes emerge temporarily. Studying these structures gives researchers an opportunity to discover materials with unique properties that are not found in their conventional forms.

Under high-vacuum conditions, the new simple cubic silver behaved differently from ordinary silver. While conventional face-centered cubic silver remained stable, simple cubic silver gradually oxidized to form silver oxide. This indicated unusually high chemical reactivity in the new structure.

"It was surprising to find that such a low-density structure could form in a pure metal crystal," says first author Dr. Masaya Sakakibara. "We expected silver nanoparticles to form when silver iodide decomposes under electron beam irradiation, but we didn't expect them to adopt a simple cubic structure."

The team used a transmission electron microscope (TEM) both to trigger the chemical transformation of silver iodide and to observe the process at the atomic scale. A TEM uses a beam of electrons with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light, allowing it to reveal individual atoms. By combining the ability to induce chemical change with real-time atomic-scale imaging, the researchers could directly observe how the new silver crystal structure emerged. "Within 100 seconds of its formation, it began to transform into silver oxide," adds Sakakibara.

"This is a new approach to discovering previously unknown crystal structures, which could also help us develop materials with novel properties in the future," says professor Yuki Kimura, co-author of the study and head of the Low Temperature Nanomaterial Science Laboratory at Hokkaido University. "Going forward, we will continue investigating the physical and chemical properties of simple cubic silver in greater detail and extend this approach to other elements and compounds."

item.title: You Likely Have Genes That Affect How Well Your Medications Work— Testing for Them Could Improve Treatment
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

All people carry differences in their DNA that could affect how they respond to medication, according to my team’s newly published research. Moreover, 1 in 4 already take a medication their body processes differently because of their genetics.

Clinicians often take a trial and error approach to prescriptions. Two people take the same medicine at the same dose. One starts feeling better, but the other experiences side effects or sees little benefit. For some medications, part of the reason behind that difference in response is written in a person’s DNA.

The field of pharmacogenomics studies how variations in your DNA contribute to how your body processes and responds to medicines. For instance, genes can influence how quickly your liver breaks down a drug and how long it stays in your bloodstream.

But using genetic testing to guide prescriptions is not yet routine. Part of the problem is a lack of large population data to study this approach more broadly. Clinicians don’t know when it’s best to order genetic testing. And because most genetic research has been done on people of European ancestry, researchers know less about how common key gene variants are in everyone else.

Genetic Variants and Drugs

To improve the diversity of pharmacogenomic data, my team of researchers and I analyzed the whole genome sequences and health records of nearly 100,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program. All of Us is an effort from the National Institutes of Health to study the health of 1 million or more people across the U.S. and its territories, with a focus on groups historically left out of biomedical research.

We examined 16 genes with well-established links to how someone responds to different medications, pairing this data with electronic health records to identify which drugs participants had already taken.

We found that every participant carried at least one relevant genetic variant, and many carried several. Around 99.5% of participants had a genetic variant for which the Food and Drug Administration or medical guidelines recommend a different drug or change in dose for certain medications.

Even more telling, about 24% had taken a drug that is affected by a genetic variant they carried. Common examples included drugs used to reduce excess stomach acid, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole, and statins used to lower cholesterol levels. Because health records can be incomplete, our results likely underestimate the actual prevalence of these gene-drug interactions.

These findings can help improve the databases clinicians and researchers use routinely in research. We identified 17,704 previously unreported variants in the regions of these genes that encode proteins. Computer models predicted that about a quarter may have significant effects on how the body processes drugs.

Our team also reported the frequencies of hundreds of genetic variants linked to drug response for people from genetic ancestries that previously had incomplete data.

Improving Precision Medicine

Overall, our research shows that DNA variation is very common, and broader genetic testing may help optimize the medications clinicians prescribe to patients. It’s also an example of how big initiatives such as the All of Us Research Program can advance precision medicine.

However, this study doesn’t prove testing would improve outcomes for each of these people. Additionally, genes are only one factor; age, kidney and liver function, and other medications also affect how the body processes drugs.

Still, I believe the direction of the research is clear. Pharmacogenomics can provide potentially relevant benefits for many people who take medications.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

Watch live on Nov. 23: Amazon launching 1st batch of internet satellites since Vulcan Centaur failure

Another batch of Amazon internet satellites will fly on Monday morning (Nov. 23), just eight days after a launch failure doomed 40 of the spacecraft.

An Ariane 6 rocket carrying 36 satellites for the Amazon Leo constellation is scheduled to lift off from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana on Monday, during a 29-minute window that opens at 6:09 a.m. EST (1109 GMT; 8:09 a.m. local time in Kourou).

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of Arianespace, the French company that operates the Ariane 6. Coverage will begin about 30 minutes before launch.

Amazon Leo, so named because it will operate in low Earth orbit, will compete with SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 operational spacecraft.

Amazon's network will eventually have more than 3,200 satellites, but just 400 or so have reached orbit to date. Another 40 were supposed to be delivered on Nov. 15, but they were lost after their rocket ride, a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan Centaur, suffered a problem shortly after launch.

Ariane 6 and Vulcan Centaur aren't the only rockets Amazon is depending on to build its broadband constellation. Jeff Bezos' company has also booked rides on ULA's Atlas V rocket, Blue Origin's New Glenn and SpaceX's Falcon 9.

Vulcan will be grounded for a while as ULA investigates the Nov. 15 failure and works to fix whatever caused it. And New Glenn hasn't flown since April, when the rocket failed to deliver AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 satellite to the proper orbit. New Glenn's return to flight was further complicated on May 28, when the rocket exploded during a routine prelaunch test.

The Ariane 6, the successor to Arianespace's Ariane 5 heavy lifter, debuted in July 2024 and has nine launches under its belt to date. All of them have been successful except that maiden mission, which was a partial failure.

Monday's mission will be the fourth Amazon Leo flight for the Ariane 6, following launches in February, April and June of this year.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz.
